challenges.name: alerting-symptoms-and-ratios-quiz
challenges.title: Which alerts should page, and what the error ratio really says
challenges.description: Decide which alerts deserve a 3am page, then compute what an error-ratio alert really returns when one small route is failing.

questions.question: Rice Rocket's on-call rule: a page must be urgent, actionable and about something users feel right now. Which of these alerts should page the on-call engineer at 3am? (Select all that apply.)
questions.explanation: Checkout 5xx ratio above 2% for 5 minutes is a symptom users feel right now (failed orders), it is urgent and someone can act on it: page. A fast error-budget burn (14.4x over both the last 1 hour and the last 5 minutes) means 2% of the whole 30-day budget is gone in an hour and the outage is still happening: page. CPU above 80% on one node is a cause, not a symptom: if users are fine it is not urgent, and if they are not, a symptom alert already fired; at most a ticket or a dashboard. A backup that finished but ran slow is real and worth a look, but nothing is broken for users tonight: open a ticket for working hours. One pod restart that Kubernetes already fixed needs no human at all; a rising restart count belongs on a dashboard or in a ticket.

options.text: Checkout error budget burning at 14.4x over both the last 1h and the last 5m
The nightly database backup finished, but took 3 hours instead of the usual 1
Pod dispatch-7f9c restarted once and is healthy again

questions.question:
During the outage, the last 5 minutes of traffic looked like this:

  route       requests   5xx
  /menu         9000       0
  /search       2400       6
  /checkout      600     150

The only error alert was:

  expr: sum(rate(http_requests_total{code=~"5.."}[5m])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total[5m])) > 0.05
  for: 5m

What does the expression return, and does the alert fire?
questions.explanation: The expression divides the total 5xx count by the total request count: 156 / 12000 = 0.013, about 1.3%, which is below 0.05, so the alert never fires while a quarter of all checkouts fail. Quiet traffic on /menu dilutes the busy failure on the small but important route. Adding by (route) to both sums keeps one ratio per route, and /checkout is 150 / 600 = 25%, far above 5%. 25% is the /checkout ratio, not what the expression returns. About 8.4% is the average of the three per-route ratios (0%, 0.25%, 25%): an average of ratios gives a tiny route the same weight as a big one, and it is not what sum()/sum() computes either. 5% is only the threshold, and for: 5m does not change the value, only how long it must stay above the threshold.

options.text: About 25%: it fires, because /checkout is far above 5%
About 8.4%: it fires, because the average error ratio of the routes is above 5%
About 1.3%: it never fires; with sum by (route) the /checkout ratio would be 25%
Exactly 5%: it stays pending forever because of for: 5m

challenges.name: fix-flapping-alert-evaluator
challenges.title: Stop the CPU alert from paging every few minutes
challenges.description: evaluate(rule, series) replays one metric series (one value per minute) through an alert rule and lists the pages it would send. The on-call review uses it to tune rules, but it has the same bugs as last night's alert: a pending alert is never dropped when the value dips back under the threshold, so short spikes add up and fire, and a firing alert resolves the moment the value is not above the threshold, so a metric hovering around 80 pages again and again. Fix it so the replay follows the rules in the docstring: fire only after the condition has been true for for_minutes minutes in a row (starting again from zero after any false minute), and resolve only when the value drops below clear_below. The runner at the bottom (do not change it) prints the alerts with fired_at and resolved_at and the number of pages.

tests.name: Night CPU from the incident: for 5m and clear below 70 turn the flapping into one page
Spikes shorter than for_minutes never page, even when they keep coming back
for_minutes 0 pages at once; a value between clear_below and threshold keeps it firing
Exactly threshold is not above it, exactly clear_below does not resolve, still firing at the end
Two real incidents in one night give two pages, each with its own resolve minute
